content_preview.summary: GitHub's October 12 changelog says it now records the authenticated pusher of each commit and adds a ruleset condition that blocks mismatched committers, in a limited public preview for Enterprise.

## Overview

GitHub published a changelog entry on October 12, 2026 titled "Push attribution for commits in limited public preview." According to the [GitHub changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-12-push-attribution-public-preview), GitHub "now durably records the authenticated user who pushed each commit and surfaces that pusher identity in the UI and API alongside the existing author and committer fields." editor_notes.source_verification: Read both gzipped snapshots from sources/2026-10/<slug>/ (manifest: both status 200, file set, suspicious_patterns null, no archive fallback). Decompressed sha256 of each snapshot matches the manifest. source-0.html.gz (github.blog changelog 2026-10-12, 'Push attribution for commits in limited public preview', 'Release', 1 minute read, labels 'application security' and 'platform governance'): contains the full entry body, not just page chrome. Verified verbatim: 'now durably records the authenticated user who pushed each commit and surfaces that pusher identity in the UI and API alongside the existing author and committer fields'; 'evading review policies and confusing audit trails'; 'GitHub already authenticates pushes'; 'is available now as a limited public preview for GitHub Enterprise customers'; contact your account team to request access; the rule 'Committer must match pusher' blocks pushes where the committer metadata does not match any verified email address of the authenticated pusher, and 'This closes a path for commit identity spoofing'; add the rule 'to a ruleset'; 'Learn more about configuring push rulesets' (link target about-rulesets#push-rulesets). TITLE QUOTE CHECK: the exact string 'Committer must match pusher' appears verbatim in the snapshot (twice, set off as its own styled element) and is described as 'A new repository rule condition' and later as 'rule'; it is therefore the name of a rule condition, and the quoted string in the title is verbatim. The snapshot uses a curly apostrophe in 'doesn't' (not in the quoted name); the body paraphrases that sentence, which is fine. 'Limited Public Preview' matches the entry's 'limited public preview' (capitalized per title style); 'Pusher Identity' matches 'pusher identity'; 'Enterprise customers' matches 'GitHub Enterprise customers' (the entry names no plan beyond that, and the article correctly lists GHES as unstated). Absences confirmed by reading the snapshot: no GA date, no pricing, no mention of GitHub Enterprise Server or Cloud, no statement on commits pushed before the preview, no treatment of bots/GitHub Apps/automation, no API field names (only 'UI and API'), no statement of which ruleset types accept the condition. source-1.html.gz (docs.github.com, available rules for rulesets): full page body. Verified verbatim: 'create push rulesets to block pushes to a private or internal repository and that repository's entire fork network'; 'For push rulesets, bypass permissions apply to a repository and the repository's entire fork network'; 'Require signed commits' rule text 'contributors and bots can only push commits that have been signed and verified to the branch'. Case-insensitive search for 'pusher' in the snapshot returns 0 hits, so the article's statement that the page does not contain the term is accurate (dated October 13, 2026). Live re-fetch via curl on 2026-10-13 (after submission): both pages returned HTTP 200 with byte-identical sha256 to the stored snapshots (changelog 4a4a38d0..., docs bec73a1a...), so no post-submission edits; 0 'pusher' hits in the live docs page. Both domains (github.blog, docs.github.com) are already in config/source_allowlist.txt; no allowlist changes. No snapshot was missing or chrome-only; no WebFetch fallback needed.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All specifics trace to the two snapshots. The date October 12, 2026, the entry title, labels, quotes and the availability statement all match. Minor glosses, not worth a correction: the article says a 'repository owner' can add the rule where the source says 'You'; the article uses 'ruleset condition' while the source says 'repository rule condition' and 'rule'. The comparison of 'Require signed commits' (cryptographic signature check) with the new condition (committer vs verified emails of the pusher) is the article's own contrast and is accurate to both pages; the article states the changelog does not say whether they are meant to be used together. The Analysis paragraph is framed as open questions, not asserted fact.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and attributed throughout; no sensationalism, no AI self-reference. Title 'Opens ... to Enterprise Customers' is a fair rendering of a limited preview that customers request via their account team, and the title states 'Limited Public Preview'.
